title: Molecular Epidemiology of Drug-Resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis in Rural South Africa: An Interpretable Machine-Learning Analysis of Routine Diagnostic Data
content: Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) remains a major challenge to tuberculosis control, particularly in high-burden settings such as South Africa. Routine molecular diagnostic assays generate quantitative cycle threshold (Ct)-derived measurements from established resistance-associated targets; however, the extent to which these routinely generated data can be computationally characterized to distinguish molecular resistance profiles remains insufficiently explored. This study evaluated Ct-derived molecular markers associated with first- and second-line anti-tuberculosis drug-resistance classifications among Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates from rural Eastern Cape, South Africa, using interpretable statistical modelling and machine-learning approaches. A retrospective analytical study was conducted using 2430 culture-confirmed M. tuberculosis specimens obtained from the National Health Laboratory Service. Ct-derived measurements for katG, inhA, gyrA, and rrs were analyzed using logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting, support vector machine, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and a multilayer perceptron neural network. Binary classification models were evaluated for isoniazid (INH), ethionamide (ETH), fluoroquinolones (FLQ), amikacin (AMK), capreomycin (CAP), and kanamycin (KAN), as well as multiclass resistance-profile classification. Among evaluable isolates, molecular resistance classifications were observed in 72.2% for INH, 31.1% for ETH, 13.2% for FLQ, and 6.9% each for AMK, CAP, and KAN. Random forest achieved the highest performance for five of the six binary classifications, whereas extra trees performed best for CAP. ROC-AUC values ranged from 0.994 to 1.000, with classification accuracies of 98.0–99.7%. Random forest also achieved the highest multiclass accuracy (98.4%), weighted F1-score (98.3%), and weighted ROC-AUC (0.999). Permutation feature importance predominantly identified katG-derived Ct measurements for INH, inhA for ETH, gyrA for FLQ, and rrs for AMK, CAP, and KAN, consistent with established molecular resistance relationships. The very high discriminatory performance should be interpreted in the context of the shared molecular-diagnostic origin of the Ct-derived predictors and resistance classifications, and therefore does not establish independent prediction of phenotypic resistance or the discovery of novel genetic determinants. Rather, these findings demonstrate that interpretable computational approaches can characterise and rank resistance-associated patterns embedded within routinely generated molecular diagnostic data, with potential utility for secondary analysis and molecular surveillance. Independent validation using phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing and/or genomic reference data is required to determine whether these approaches provide incremental predictive or clinical value beyond the underlying molecular assay.
